t:
That all conveyances, including oil and gas or mineral leases, by Indians of the Five Civilized Tribes in Oklahoma of lands acquired by inheritance or devise, made after the effective date of the Act of January 27, 1933, and prior to the effective date of this Act, that were approved either by a county court in Oklahoma or by the Secretary of the Interior are hereby validated and confirmed:
Provided, That if any such conveyance is subject to attack upon grounds other than sufficiency of approval or lack of approval thereof, such conveyance shall not be affected by this Act.

fable.w: The section retroactively validates past conveyances by Indians of the Five Civilized Tribes that a county court or the Secretary of the Interior had already approved. The tempting reading is that the references to approval and to conveyances being "subject to attack" amount to outside-party involvement or a right to sue. That reading fails because the approvals are past case-by-case actions on private transactions, and the proviso only preserves existing grounds for challenging private conveyances rather than granting a right to sue the federal government. The section requires no consultation, hearing, comment period, rulemaking or advisory body before any future federal decision.
fable.s: that were approved either by a county court in Oklahoma or by the Secretary of the Interior are hereby validated and confirmed

qwen_block.w: This section validates past conveyances that were already approved by courts or the Secretary of the Interior. It does not establish a new process for public participation, consultation, or advisory input into a future federal decision. The approval mentioned is a past administrative or judicial act, not a current requirement for outside participation.
qwen_block.s: That all conveyances, including oil and gas or mineral leases, by Indians of the Five Civilized Tribes in Oklahoma of lands acquired by inheritance or devise, made after the effective date of the Act of January 27, 1933, and prior to the effective date of this Act, that were approved either by a county court in Oklahoma or by the Secretary of the Interior are hereby validated and confirmed

opus.w: The section simply confirms past conveyances that a county court or the Secretary already approved. No outside party is consulted on, or takes part in, a future federal decision. The county court approvals are past events, and the proviso only leaves other existing challenges in place rather than granting an outside party a right to sue over a federal decision. There is also no hearing, comment period, advisory body, or rulemaking.
opus.s: Provided, That if any such conveyance is subject to attack upon grounds other than sufficiency of approval or lack of approval thereof, such conveyance shall not be affected by this Act.
opus.b: 1. **Tempting reading:** The section mentions approval "by a county court in Oklahoma," a body outside the federal government, and conveyances that may be "subject to attack." Both could look like outside participation or a right to sue. That reading doesn't hold up. The county court approvals already happened, and they were approvals of private land transfers, not input into a future federal decision. The proviso only keeps existing challenges available; it does not give anyone a new right to sue over a federal decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section validates past conveyances that were already approved by county courts or the Secretary of the Interior. It does not require the federal government to consult with or coordinate with outside parties (such as the county courts or the Indians) to make a new decision. The validation is a unilateral legislative act confirming prior approvals, not a participatory process.
qwen_chat.s: That all conveyances... are hereby validated and confirmed: Provided, That if any such conveyance is subject to attack upon grounds other than sufficiency of approval or lack of approval thereof, such conveyance shall not be affected by this Act.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the validation of conveyances approved by a "county court" implies participation because county courts are local government entities. However, the text does not require the federal government to consult with the county court; rather, it retroactively validates actions that were already approved by either a county court or the Secretary of the Interior. The federal government is not engaging in a decision-making process involving outside parties; it is simply confirming past legal transactions. There is no requirement for consultation, coordination, or input from outside parties in the current federal decision.
